newsitem.title: UK: UK's OFT mulls new approach to vertical restraint.
newsitem.headline: UK's OFT mulls new approach to vertical restraint.

text.p: Restrictions between firms at different stages of production and distribution can harm competition, according to a research paper published on Wednesday by Britain's Office of Fair Trading (OFT).

The paper, "Vertical Restraints and Competition Policy' by Paul Dobson of Nottingham University and Michael Waterson of Warwick University, said vertical restraints can undermine competition if one or more of the firms involved possesses market power and that can outweigh any efficiency gains.

Vertical restraints include refusing to supply certain retailers, requiring retailers to stock only one manufacturer's goods and tying sales of one good to another. Dobson and Waterson said they need to be looked at on a case-by-case basis.

They proposed a new investigation procedure to assist in answering three key questions: whether firms have market power, what the effects on competition are and whether the vertical restraint creates efficiency gains.
"There has been much debate about the effects of vertical restraints," said John Bridgeman, Director General of Fair Trading.

"We are now looking to see how we can incorporate the approach proposed by the authors into our own assessments of vertical restraints. This will, I hope, produce a more systematic and effective application of competition policy in this important area."

The European Commission is also reviewing its policy towards vertical restraints and intends to publish a Green Paper next year before reviewing existing block exemptions for certain vertical agreements, said Bridgeman.

The research was commissioned by the OFT following a number of major monopoly inquiries involving vertical restraints during the early 1990s, including reports on the beer industry, the supply of petrol and the supply of national newspapers.
